# The design rubric

<!-- Generated by scripts/export_rubric.py from src/langwich/quality.py. Do not edit by hand. -->

`langwich validate FILE` answers one question: will this sheet work? The file matches the
contract, nothing is broken, no answer is given away. The design rubric answers the next one —
is it a well-made lesson? — as far as that can be **measured**.

```bash
langwich validate data/night_trains_en_de.json --quality            # the report, then the findings
langwich validate data/night_trains_en_de.json --quality --prompt   # … as a repair prompt for the AI
langwich validate data/night_trains_en_de.json --quality --strict   # exit status 1 on any finding
langwich validate data/night_trains_en_de.json --quality --json     # findings and measures as JSON
```

Every rule is a pure function of the worksheet JSON: no AI reads the sheet, nothing is fetched,
nothing is random. The same file gets the same findings, in the same order, on every machine.
That is what makes the rubric usable as a test.

## What it is for

- **A worksheet you just made.** Run it with `--quality`. A finding says where (a JSON pointer),
  what is wrong and what to do; `--prompt` hands all of them to the AI that wrote the file.
- **A change to the brief.** Write the same story with the old and the new brief and compare the
  findings and the measures (`--json` prints both): words per sentence, share of direct speech,
  number of items, how many tasks can be checked against the key.
- **A new kind of task.** `KIND_DESIGN` in `langwich.quality` holds one entry per task kind: what
  is counted, how many of it one task should have, and how the learner checks the answer. A kind
  without an entry fails the tests, and so does an entry that no real task lives up to. A new
  exercise concept has to say what good looks like before it ships.
- **The bundled examples.** `tests/test_quality.py` holds every example to every rule. Findings
  that are known and tolerated are listed there in `ACCEPTED`, each with a reason; the test fails
  on a finding that is not listed, and on a listed finding that no longer occurs. So the list can
  only shrink. To raise the bar, add a rule, give it a broken example in `MUTANTS` (a rule without
  one fails the suite), and fix or list what it finds.

## What it cannot see

Whether the facts are true. Whether the language is natural and right for the level. Whether the
reader wants to know how the story ends. No deterministic rule can judge these; they stay with
the author and the reviewer (the `/langwich` command reviews them in step 5). A sheet without
findings is well built, not necessarily good.

## The 50 rules

Where a number comes from the authoring brief (`langwich prompt`), the reason says so; the level table is read from the brief's own, so the two cannot drift apart. The other rules are common item-writing practice.

### Story (16)

The shape of the story: beats, a protagonist who is there from the first scene to the last, direct speech, scenes of similar weight, sentences that fit the level, facts beside the story rather than inside it.

| Rule | What good looks like | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `beat-missing` | every scene names its beat | the brief asks for one beat per scene; without it nothing can check the story's shape |
| `beat-order` | the story opens with the setup and its beats never go backwards | setup → development → complication → climax → resolution is the arc a reader follows |
| `no-turn` | a story of three or more scenes has a complication or a climax | without something going wrong there is a report, not a story |
| `no-resolution` | the last scene resolves the story | the learner reads to find out how it ends |
| `protagonist-absent` | the protagonist is named in the first scene, the last scene and most others | one person to follow from the goal to the payoff |
| `character-unused` | every character on the cover is named in the story | the cover introduces the cast; a name that never comes up is a loose end |
| `logline-without-protagonist` | the logline names the protagonist | the logline says who wants what; the first character it names is the one the story rules follow |
| `no-direct-speech` | at least half of the scenes contain direct speech | the brief asks for some direct speech in each scene: facts arrive through people, not through a narrator's lecture |
| `scene-unbalanced` | no scene is more than twice as long as the shortest | each scene is one sitting of reading followed by its tasks |
| `sentence-length` | sentences fit the level: the mean stays under the level's limit and no sentence is twice as long | the brief's level table (A1 4–8 words, A2 5–12, B1 up to about 15) |
| `translation-missing` | every scene has a complete translation | the translations are printed with the solutions; a missing or cut-off one leaves the learner without a check |
| `fact-repeats-story` | a 'Did you know?' fact tells something the story has not already told | the brief: short, surprising, true, not already told by the story |
| `fact-unanchored` | every fact is placed beside a scene | a fact belongs next to the moment of the story it explains |
| `fact-too-long` | a fact has at most three sentences | a sidebar, not a second text to read |
| `cover-incomplete` | the cover has a standfirst, a setting and at least two characters with roles | the cover sets the stakes before the first line |
| `series-without-teaser` | an episode of a series ends with a teaser for the next one | the hook is what makes a series a series |

### Lesson (13)

The arc of the sheet: every phase present, every scene checked, the key words pre-taught, recycled and finally written by the learner, every grammar point practised, a mix of task kinds.

| Rule | What good looks like | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `no-warm-up` | the sheet starts with a warm-up task | the key words are met before the story needs them |
| `no-language-work` | the sheet has a form or practice task | understanding the story is not yet using its language |
| `scene-unchecked` | every scene is followed by a comprehension or picture task about it | read a little, check what happened, read on |
| `task-variety` | a sheet of seven or more tasks uses at least five kinds, and none of them for more than 40% of the tasks | different kinds train different things; the same kind again and again is a drill |
| `target-not-pretaught` | at least half of the key words appear in the warm-up | the brief's first task: the key words with their meanings |
| `target-thinly-practised` | every key word comes up in at least three tasks | the brief asks for the story and three tasks; a word met once is not learned |
| `target-never-produced` | every key word is written by the learner at least once | recognising a word is not yet being able to use it |
| `grammar-unpractised` | every grammar point is practised by a form or practice task that names it | a grammar box without a task beside it is decoration |
| `grammar-few-examples` | every grammar point has at least two examples | the brief asks for two or three; one example is an instance, two show the pattern |
| `practice-leaves-story` | practice clozes and dialogues name a character of the story | practice continues the story in new sentences, it does not leave it |
| `comprehension-quotes-story` | comprehension items paraphrase the story instead of quoting it | a statement copied from the text tests finding, not understanding |
| `labels-unused` | a picture with labels has a label task | numbered markers without a task are numbers on a picture |
| `answer-missing` | every task the learner can get wrong has an answer in the key | a sheet for self-study is only as good as its answer key |

### Items (21)

The craft of the single task: enough items and not too many, true/false with both kinds, options of similar length, spare words in every word box, nothing in the task that shows its own answer, room to write.

| Rule | What good looks like | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `item-count` | a task has a sensible number of items for its kind | too few is not practice, too many is a chore; the ranges are in KIND_DESIGN |
| `tf-one-sided` | a true/false task has both kinds, and neither makes up more than three quarters | a pattern the learner can guess needs no reading |
| `tf-correction-same` | the correction of a false statement differs from the statement | the answer key must show what is true instead |
| `mc-few-options` | a multiple-choice question has at least three options | with two options a guess is right half the time |
| `mc-answer-stands-out` | the right option is not far longer than every wrong one | the longest, most careful option is the first thing a test-wise learner ticks |
| `mc-longest-is-right` | across a task the right option is the longest in at most half of the questions | the same cue, as a pattern over the whole task |
| `match-no-spare` | a matching task has at least one spare answer | otherwise the last pair is free |
| `match-trivial-pair` | the two sides of a pair are not the same word | a pair that matches itself teaches nothing |
| `cloze-too-dense` | a gap text keeps at least five words of context per gap (three in a form drill) | a gap is filled from its context; without context it is a guess |
| `bank-distractors` | a word box has at least one spare word, and fewer spare words than gaps | one spare word keeps the last gap honest; too many turn the box into noise |
| `bank-word-twice` | each word-box word fills exactly one gap | the box shows a word once; needing it twice leaves a gap without a word |
| `distractor-stands-out` | a spare word does not differ from every answer by its capital letter | the brief: capitals and endings reveal nothing |
| `answer-shown-in-task` | a gap's answer does not stand elsewhere in the same task | the brief: the answer appears nowhere else in the task |
| `lines-too-few` | there is room to write: a line per twelve words of a model answer, a line per ten words of a text | the sheet is worked through with a pen |
| `writing-scaffold` | a writing task has a starter, three or more words to use, a word range that fits the level and a model answer | a blank page is the hardest task on the sheet; the scaffold makes it doable |
| `must-use-unseen` | the words a writing task asks for have come up on the sheet: in the story, a fact, the word list, a grammar box or another task | the learner can only use what the sheet has taught |
| `transform-no-change` | a transformed sentence differs from its prompt | otherwise there is nothing to do |
| `word-building-unrelated` | a built word contains its parts | the learner assembles the answer from what is given |
| `media-search-thin` | a media search gives search terms, not links, and at least two questions | links rot; search terms in the target language are the task |
| `label-crowded` | the markers of a picture do not sit on top of each other | a number has to point at one thing |
| `title-generic` | every task has its own title that belongs to the story | the brief: 'Thursday: a second chance', never 'Exercise 3' |

## Task kinds

What is counted in a task of each kind, how many of it a task should have (`item-count`), and how the learner checks the work.

| Kind | Counted | Sensible range | The learner checks against |
|---|---|---|---|
| `match` | pairs | 4–12 | one right answer in the key |
| `true_false` | statements | 3–6 | one right answer in the key |
| `multiple_choice` | questions | 2–6 | one right answer in the key |
| `order_events` | events | 4–7 | one right answer in the key |
| `questions` | questions | 1–6 | a model answer to compare with |
| `cloze` | gaps | 3–12 | one right answer in the key |
| `transform` | sentences | 3–8 | one right answer in the key |
| `word_building` | words | 3–8 | one right answer in the key |
| `label` | labels | 4–8 | one right answer in the key |
| `writing` | texts | 1 | a model answer to compare with |
| `dialogue` | gaps and lines to write | 3–12 | a model answer to compare with |
| `media_search` | search terms | 2–4 | nothing to compare (the learner's own find or drawing) |
| `draw` | words to label | 3–8 | nothing to compare (the learner's own find or drawing) |

## Level limits

`sentence-length` and `writing-scaffold` scale with the CEFR level. The writing range is the brief's; a task may leave it by half at the lower end and by half at the upper end before the rule reports it.

| Level | Words per sentence (mean, at most) | Longest sentence (at most) | Writing task (words) |
|---|---|---|---|
| A1 | 8 | 16 | 25–40 |
| A2 | 12 | 24 | 40–70 |
| B1 | 15 | 30 | 60–100 |
| B2 | 20 | 40 | 100–150 |
| C1 | 25 | 50 | 150–220 |
| C2 | 30 | 60 | 180–260 |
